newsitem.title: UK: Owen quits NatWest Markets major overhaul.
newsitem.headline: Owen quits NatWest Markets major overhaul.

text.p: Britain's NatWest Bank said Monday its investment banking boss Martin Owen had quit amid a major overhaul of the business which was draining the group's profits.
NatWest's Chief Executive Derek Wanless said he had not fallen out with Owen and the decision that a change of leadership was needed had been taken by them both after lengthy discussions.
Shares in the bank ended the day down 43-1/2 British pence (71 cents) at 753 pence ($12.30).
Owen's future has been under a cloud since late February when NatWest Markets disclosed it had sustained multi-million dollar losses over a two-year period in its derivatives division.

Wanless blamed a significant fall in NatWest Markets' profits -- which will also hit the group's results for the first half of the year -- on the fall-out of the 90 million pounds ($147 million) interest rate options loss.
But Owen's departure also coincides with a major shift in focus by NatWest Markets, which had spent huge sums in its pursuit of becoming one of the top 10 global investment banking firms.
The bank, and Wanless, have been under intense pressure from institutional investors to improve returns, with investment banking seen as a drain.
While analysts were not surprised by Owen's resignation, they were disappointed NatWest did not give greater detail of the proposed changes.

Wanless said the group would redeploy capital away from areas such as the loan market, where banks lend huge sums at increasingly tight margins, to areas such as wealth management which generate regular fee income without being capital intensive.
Owen has been head of the investment bank since 1992 and has masterminded, with Wanless's backing, a string of important acquisitions.

Natwest also disclosed the full impact of the interest rate options losses uncovered in February by warning profits for the whole group for the first half of the year would not exceed 770 million British pounds ($1.3 billion).

Banking analysts had expected a considerably better figure for the six months to the end of June, with one forecasting pre-tax profits in the region of 900 million ($1.47 billion) pounds before the warning.
